AUS.mechanism: An institution that can reassign its own staff answers a complaint by moving the person, which keeps him in work and keeps the complaint out of the police system — and the same belief that an authority knows better than a family let the state move children too.
AUS.story:
A Catholic bishop decides which priest serves in which parish, and may move a priest at any time without saying why. By late 1975 Bishop Ronald Mulkearns of Ballarat, in the Australian state of Victoria, knew that one of his priests, Gerald Ridsdale, was abusing children. He did not go to the police. He gave Ridsdale another parish, then another — about thirteen postings between 1962 and 1991. Each move settled the bishop's problem rather than the children's: the complaint stayed inside the church, no public case opened, and the priest kept a job that put him beside families who had never heard the earlier reports. A police officer accepted the bishop's promise to handle it himself. Ridsdale was first convicted in 1993, eighteen years after the bishop knew, and was eventually convicted of abusing more than 70 children. A national inquiry with the power to compel documents and sworn testimony, the Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse, which sat from 2013 to 2017, called that a catastrophic failure. It also found that in 1972, in the same diocese, a senior police officer had offered a detective a promotion to drop an investigation into a monsignor.

A move across a border is much harder to reverse. In March 2008, after a teacher confronted the headmistress of Melbourne's ultra-Orthodox Adass Israel School, the school arranged and paid for a 1:20 a.m. flight to Israel for Malka Leifer and four of her children, and told police nothing until she had gone. Australia issued a warrant in 2014 for 74 offences involving at least eight pupils. Getting her back then depended on extradition, one country asking another to hand a suspect over and the second country's courts deciding whether to agree. Israel's deputy health minister at the time, Yaakov Litzman, pressured ministry staff to alter psychiatric assessments so that she would appear too unwell for an extradition hearing. She was extradited in January 2021 and convicted in April 2023 of 18 charges including rape; Litzman later pleaded guilty to breach of trust.

Australian governments removed children themselves on a related belief. Between roughly 1910 and 1970 Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children were taken into institutions, missions and non-Indigenous homes; the 1997 Bringing Them Home report estimated that between one in three and one in ten Indigenous children were removed. From the late 1950s to the 1970s tens of thousands of babies born to unmarried, mostly teenage mothers were taken for adoption, often without informed consent — the signature existed, the choice did not.

Australia's file is unusually detailed because one inquiry examined churches, schools and state institutions together and could demand their records. When you read about an abuser here, read the list of postings rather than the crimes: every transfer was a decision by a named person who already knew. Ask who was told first, and what that person did the following week.

NLD.mechanism: A receiving country's adoption system ran for thirty years on documents nobody verified, so the fraud was committed at the far end and the signature at home made it lawful.
NLD.story:
An adoption from another country needs a signature at both ends. A Dutch couple applies, an intermediary licensed by the Dutch justice ministry works with an intermediary in the sending country, and somewhere in the file is a paper saying the child has no parent able to raise them. Everything rests on that paper being true, and for decades nobody in the Netherlands checked whether it was.

In the 1980s about 4,000 babies reached Dutch families from Sri Lanka. A Dutch documentary reported in 2017 that babies had been bought or taken from hospitals, handed to women paid to pose as their mothers, and sold for adoption. The paid mother is the crucial part, because it meant a Sri Lankan court watched a woman consent to give up her own child, which is precisely what a court looks for. Sri Lanka's health minister said on camera that there had been a lot of baby farms in those years.

A commission chaired by Tjibbe Joustra, set up in 2019 to examine the Dutch side, reported in February 2021. It found serious violations in adoptions from Sri Lanka, Indonesia, Bangladesh, Brazil and Colombia between 1967 and the late 1990s, and concluded that the Dutch government had failed for decades to prevent them. The government then acknowledged that its own officials had known of wrongdoing for years without intervening. It suspended every intercountry adoption with immediate effect on 8 February 2021 and announced in May 2024 that Dutch citizens would no longer be allowed to adopt from abroad.

The church kept its own silence. A commission the Dutch Catholic Church appointed under the former minister Wim Deetman reported in December 2011 that at least 800 priests, monks and other religious had abused children between 1945 and 1985, with an estimated 10,000 to 20,000 minors abused. Bishops knew, and followed what the report called a policy of not hanging out the dirty washing. A diocese that reports its own priest loses standing, donations and recruits, and gains nothing countable.

The country's third role is landlord. For years the Netherlands hosted more of the material the Internet Watch Foundation removed than anywhere else — 47 per cent in 2018, down to 11 per cent, or 33,788 web addresses, in 2025. Hosting means renting space on a computer permanently connected to the internet, and the Dutch market is large, fast and cheap, so it draws customers from everywhere. Allegations in the Netherlands against Joris Demmink were investigated and never led to a charge; they remain unproven.

Two of these failures look alike from the inside: a church guarding its name, and a ministry stamping files it never audited. When a country ranks high as a host, ask whether the offenders are there or only the servers. When you see an adoption file, ask which claim in it was ever checked by someone with no stake in the placement going through.

IRL.mechanism: Handling a complaint inside the church's own courts ends the matter instead of starting a case, and even the state inquiries that later forced the files open could be bargained down over what they were allowed to publish.
IRL.story:
In 1975 two teenage boys were brought before a church inquiry in Ireland and made to swear oaths of silence about what Father Brendan Smyth had done to them. One of the clergymen present, Seán Brady, later became a Cardinal. An inquiry of that kind runs under the church's own law: it can question people and move a priest, but it produces no charge, no court record and nothing police can use. Swearing the boys to silence turned the only evidence into something that could not travel. Smyth's order, the Norbertines, knew his history and moved him between parishes, dioceses and countries, including the United States, sometimes without warning the local bishop; the BBC put the number of children he abused at at least 143. When police in Northern Ireland asked for him to be handed over, the Irish Attorney General's office let the request sit, and the row over the delay brought down the government in 1994. He was jailed in Northern Ireland that year, sentenced in Dublin in 1997 to twelve years, and died in prison weeks later.

When the state looked, it found the habit everywhere. The Murphy Report of 2009 found that four successive Dublin archbishops had failed to tell the Gardaí, the Irish police, what they knew, and that the archdiocese had been buying insurance against abuse claims since 1987 — an organisation treating the abuse as a predictable cost rather than something to stop.

The Ryan Commission spent nine years, to 2009, on more than 250 church-run institutions that had held over 30,000 children, and found sexual abuse endemic in the boys' institutions, most run by the Christian Brothers. State education inspectors had visited and had not stopped it. In 2004 the Christian Brothers sued the commission to keep their members' names out of the report and won: the 2,600-page report identifies no abuser, and its findings cannot be used to prosecute anyone.

The Mother and Baby Homes Commission reported in January 2021 on institutions that held about 56,000 unmarried women and 57,000 children between 1922 and 1998 and doubled as adoption agencies. About 9,000 of those children died there, about 15 per cent of all the children in those institutions, at about double the national infant death rate. In 2018 the state child agency Tusla referred 126 births that one adoption agency, St Patrick's Guild, had registered falsely, recording adoptive parents as birth parents. A false registration is the surest way to make a transfer permanent, because the child's origin stops existing on paper.

Ireland's file is long because Ireland looked early and looked hard, not because it was worse than its neighbours. The same orders appear in the abuse, the adoptions and the deaths, and police, school inspectors and the Attorney General's office each had a turn to act. When an inquiry report names no perpetrator, ask who went to court to arrange that.

RUS.mechanism: One state can close the route by which children leave and open the route by which children arrive, and both decisions turn on something other than the children.
RUS.story:
Between 1994 and 2014 the United States issued 60,266 immigrant visas to children adopted from Russia, the largest year being 2004 with 5,865. Then the route closed. In April 2010 an American adoptive mother put her seven-year-old adopted son on a one-way flight back to Moscow alone. On 28 December 2012 President Putin signed a law banning adoption by US citizens from the following January. It was named after Dima Yakovlev, a Russian toddler who died in 2008 after his American adoptive father left him for hours in a hot car; the father was found not guilty of involuntary manslaughter. The law was widely read as a reply to the US Magnitsky Act, signed a fortnight earlier. That is worth holding on to when any country closes an adoption programme: a closure can be a diplomatic move rather than a finding about how children were treated, and nothing about the system itself was investigated when it shut.

Children already inside Russian institutions were in another position. Human Rights Watch visited ten state orphanages for children with disabilities and reported in 2014, after more than 200 interviews, that staff beat children, gave them sedative injections and sent them to psychiatric hospitals as punishment, and that children judged most severely disabled lay all day in cribs, often tied to the furniture. They had almost no way to tell anyone outside, and health workers pressed parents to give up disabled newborns, which is how such institutions stay full.

After February 2022 the movement reversed. A decree of 30 May 2022 made it easier to give Ukrainian children Russian citizenship so Russian families could adopt them; Russia opened a register of families wanting one and paid families for each adopted child granted citizenship. The payment is what turns a policy into a volume of placements. The children's rights commissioner, Maria Lvova-Belova, said she had adopted a child from Mariupol herself, and her own bulletin recorded 380 orphans placed with Russian foster families and about 2,000 children moved out of institutions in February 2022. Yale researchers reported at least 43 camps in Russia and Crimea holding at least 6,000 Ukrainian children for what Russia called re-education. On 17 March 2023 the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Putin and Lvova-Belova for the war crimes of unlawful deportation and transfer of children; the court has no police of its own, so a warrant is an instruction to member states to arrest him if he enters their territory. Ukraine's official count of deported children stands at 20,651, and UN monitors verified 122 abductions, two of those children since returned to their families.

Russia shows that the direction children travel tells you less than the paperwork and the payments behind them. When a government says it is protecting children, check what else was signed that month, and check who is paid for each child placed.

KHM.mechanism: Pressure in one place moves the trade to the next place, and a raid announced in advance moves the children before it arrives.
KHM.story:
Through 1992 and 1993 roughly 22,000 UN personnel arrived in Cambodia for the peacekeeping mission known as UNTAC. Across those two years the estimated number of sex workers in the country rose from about 6,000 to more than 25,000. Several thousand foreign men on salaries is demand, and demand gets supplied locally. The UN kept no proper record of allegations at the time, which is why the figures come from academics reconstructing it later, and the sources consulted document no findings about children against UNTAC staff.

Svay Pak, a poor fishing village on the edge of Phnom Penh, became known over the following decade as a place where foreign men bought sex with children, most of them ethnic Vietnamese girls sold by families with nothing. Observers connected its growth to Thailand's crackdown on child prostitution in the 1990s: the buyers had not stopped travelling, they had changed destination. On 22 January 2003 police raided Svay Pak. The raid had been advertised in advance, nearly every child had already been moved to Siem Reap and Sihanoukville, and no pimp or client was arrested. Local officials had been taking money from the brothel owners, which tells you who held both the information and a reason to pass it on. The government closed the brothels in 2005 and the business reopened in massage parlours and karaoke bars, where there is no street to raid. Survey estimates of the share of minors among Cambodia's sex workers fell from nearly 35 per cent to 1 or 2 per cent by 2017.

Some buyers were dealt with by their own countries, which had given their courts power to try citizens for sex offences committed abroad. Ronald Boyajian, already a registered sex offender in California, was arrested in Cambodia in 2009 on what prosecutors called his thirty-fifth trip to Asia in nine years, and was sentenced in the United States to 70 years over a nine-year-old girl in Svay Pak.

Adoption was a separate exit. Between 1997 and 2001 the American facilitator Lauryn Galindo arranged about 800 adoptions for US families, more than half of all adoptions out of Cambodia; the US government said her business paid Cambodian mothers for their babies. The United States stopped Cambodian adoptions in late 2001, and in 2004 Galindo pleaded guilty to visa fraud and money laundering, admitting she had falsified documents that erased children's identities while denying trafficking. Some adoptive families later found their child had living relatives. In 2019 the US State Department reported that some Cambodian orphanages bought children from poor families and kept them in poor conditions to attract donations, which turns the idea of an orphanage inside out: the child becomes the fundraising asset.

Cambodia is this map's clearest case of displacement rather than reduction. When a district or a country is described as cleaned up, ask where the children went, and who in the local administration knew the date of the raid.

POL.mechanism: Whether a case can ever be tried depends on which state holds the accused and which archive holds the paperwork.
POL.story:
A papal nuncio is both a priest and the ambassador of the Holy See, a sovereign state with its own courts. The Polish archbishop Józef Wesołowski was nuncio to the Dominican Republic from 2008. In 2013, with allegations circulating that he had abused minors there, the Vatican recalled him; Dominican prosecutors opened their investigation that September, after he had gone. The recall put him inside the one territory whose law the Vatican controls, and the Vatican told Polish prosecutors that its law did not permit extradition, the formal handing over of a suspect to another country's courts. A church tribunal found him guilty and he was stripped of the priesthood in June 2014. A Vatican prosecutor indicted him in June 2015 over children in the Dominican Republic and over abuse images; he was found dead in his Vatican rooms that August, before trial. Three jurisdictions could have tried him; none did.

The same gap can work the other way. Father Wojciech Gil, a Polish priest who had worked in the Dominican Republic, went home to Poland, which has no extradition treaty with that country and so could not be made to send him back. Polish police arrested him anyway in February 2014 using evidence the Dominicans supplied, and in March 2015 a court in Wołomin sentenced him to seven years for abusing six minors there and two in Poland. A missing treaty does not prevent a prosecution; it only means the decision rests entirely with the home country.

Inside Poland the fight has been over who may read the files. In March 2019 the Polish bishops published their own study: 382 priests accused of abusing 625 children between 1990 and mid-2018, a count produced by the institution being counted. Two documentaries by the Sekielski brothers put the bishops' own handling of cases on screen, and Vatican investigations followed: Bishop Edward Janiak of Kalisz was made to resign and Archbishop Sławoj Leszek Głódź of Gdańsk was removed after covering up abuse by two priests. Poland created a State Commission on abuse of children under fifteen in 2019. In 2022 it was criticised over a limit it cannot lift by itself: church documents sent to the Vatican are out of its reach, and under church law files are destroyed ten years after a conviction.

Poland was also a country children were taken from. Between 1940 and 1945 the SS seized children in occupied Poland that it judged racially valuable and placed them with German families under new names — up to 200,000, by estimates reported by DW. The new names are what made those removals permanent, and why the number is still an estimate; a US military tribunal at Nuremberg convicted thirteen of fourteen SS race-office and Lebensborn officials over the kidnapping.

In each part of this record the decisive question is custody of paper: who holds the file, who may read it, how long it survives. When an institution publishes a count of its own abusers, ask which archive the counters were let into, and what the rules say about destroying records.

THA.mechanism: The offence happens in Thailand but the case is usually closed, if at all, in the buyer's own country, which has to have given its courts that power and has to choose to use it.
THA.story:
In 1996 a Swiss man already convicted of abusing children in Fribourg in 1980 and in Valais in 1991 went back to Thailand. In Pattaya he ran a bar with a hotel room used by European men. Mainly between 2002 and 2013 he abused more than 80 boys there and in Nong Hoi in the north, and made boys perform acts with European clients. He was never tried in Thailand. A Swiss court sentenced him in March 2018 to 16 years, under the kind of law that lets a country prosecute its own citizens for sex offences committed anywhere in the world. Mark Frost, a British former teacher and scout leader who had first admitted an offence in 1992, abused boys from poor families in Thailand between 2011 and 2013 and streamed the abuse by webcam to another European man; a British court gave him 13 life sentences in 2017. Britain's own national inquiry counted his as one of only about eight successful UK prosecutions since 1997 for offences committed abroad, which shows how seldom that power is actually used.
Thailand closed its own gaps earlier than most. An act of 1996 made sex with anyone under 18 inside a prostitution business an offence whatever the child was said to have consented to, which removed the defence buyers had relied on, and a 2008 act covered trafficking. In 2017 Thai officials refused entry to 74 known foreign sex offenders. The pressure from outside did not stop: Australia said about 800 of its registered child sex offenders travelled abroad in 2016, 40 per cent without telling police.

The business kept going indoors. In 2023 police raided an illegal bar on Bangla Road in Patong, Phuket, and found six people under 18 being sexually exploited. In July 2024 the Phuket Provincial Court sentenced seven defendants, Thai and foreign; the main defendant, the foreign owner, received 1,073 years in total, having first fled to a neighbouring country. Five senior Patong police officers were transferred after the raid. A transfer is not a finding of anything, but it is the question being asked out loud: what did the police on the main tourist street know about a bar on it.

A 2016 global study by the group ECPAT found that most people who travel to abuse children are domestic or regional travellers rather than Westerners, and that conviction rates are very low. So when you read that an offender was caught in Thailand, ask which country's court will actually hear it, whether that country has given itself the power, and how many times it has used it.

UGA.mechanism: An adoption order is a legal product, and a judge who can be paid produces genuine paperwork for a child who was never free to be adopted.
UGA.story:
No child leaves Uganda for adoption without a judge's order. That order is the whole transaction: once it is signed, the child's new status is lawful at both ends, and the visa officer in the receiving country sees a valid document rather than a question. Between 2013 and 2016 an Ohio agency, European Adoption Consultants, arranged the adoption of more than 30 Ugandan children by American families. The Ugandan families were told their children would be going to school in Kampala. The children were taken to an unlicensed home and then sent abroad, and bribes were paid to Ugandan judges and other officials to obtain the orders. A former agency employee, Robin Longoria, pleaded guilty in August 2019 to bribing Ugandan officials. In August 2020 a federal indictment charged two more employees and a Ugandan lawyer, Dorah Mirembe, who are accused and not convicted. The same month the US State Department imposed sanctions on two Ugandan judges, Moses Mukiibi and Wilson Musalu Musene, and on two lawyers.

Decades earlier children were taken with no paperwork at all. From 1987 the Lord's Resistance Army, led by Joseph Kony, abducted children across northern Uganda to serve as fighters, porters and what the group called wives; UNICEF estimated at least 25,000 by 2006, and some were held at the group's bases across the border in southern Sudan. In February 2021 the International Criminal Court convicted Dominic Ongwen, a brigade commander who had himself been abducted as a child, of 61 crimes including rape, sexual slavery, forced marriage and the use of children under 15 as soldiers, and sentenced him to 25 years. Kony's own arrest warrant is still outstanding, because the court has no police and depends on a state picking him up.

Ugandan soldiers sent abroad appear in the record too. Human Rights Watch documented in 2014 ten incidents of sexual abuse and fourteen of sexual exploitation by African Union troops in Mogadishu, mainly Ugandan personnel at the mission's headquarters; four rape cases and one assault involved girls under 18, the youngest a 12-year-old allegedly raped by a Ugandan soldier in May 2013. Many of the women and girls had gone to the bases seeking medicine or food, and interpreters arranged the soldiers' access. The base holds what people need, and whoever controls the gate decides the price.

In each of these the person handing the child over holds a recognised position: a judge, a commander, an elder, a soldier at a gate. When adoptions from one country rise quickly, follow the signatures rather than the children, and ask who is paid at each one.

BRA.mechanism: Nobody has ever been given the job of counting, so the record is made of the few cases that happened to reach a courtroom.
BRA.story:
Brazil has the largest Catholic population of any country, and in the sources reached here it has held no national inquiry into abuse in churches or children's institutions. That absence is worth understanding, because an inquiry is not just a louder version of a prosecution. A national inquiry can demand an institution's internal files, summon the people who ran it, and commission a survey of the general population — which reaches the large majority of survivors who never went to the police. When France did that, its inquiry estimated about 216,000 minors abused by clergy and religious since 1950, against about 3,000 identified before. Same country, same church, a number roughly seventy times larger, because the method of counting changed. Brazil has no figure of that kind, and what is known has arrived one case at a time, through individual prosecutions and a parliamentary hearing in 2010 about a single priest.

On the coast the pattern is tourism, and it runs through ordinary jobs. In 2006 Brazil's Federal Police described sex tourism as most frequent in Fortaleza, Recife, Salvador and Natal, and ran periodic raids, including one on a nightclub in Ponta Negra, Natal, where 110 foreigners were present and no children were found that night. A law passed in 2000 set four to ten years for subjecting a child or adolescent to prostitution. The 2025 US trafficking report says taxi drivers and hotel, bar and nightclub staff in coastal resorts arrange child sex trafficking. Those are the people a visitor asks for what he wants, which is why they matter more than whoever owns the building. The report cites a study suggesting that up to 16 per cent of girls aged 14 to 17 in one northeastern metropolitan area were likely victims of commercial sexual exploitation. It also records no investigations of officials suspected of involvement, and a 2016 child sex-trafficking case involving an elected official in Paraná still unresolved.

Some cases are finished elsewhere entirely. Warren Scott Kennell, an American missionary with New Tribes Mission, abused Katukina girls while posted in the Brazilian Amazon; he was arrested when he landed at Orlando airport and jailed for 58 years in 2014. In 2021 a Dutch inquiry found serious violations in adoptions from Brazil between 1967 and 1998 — a finding about Brazilian children made by the receiving country rather than here.

A thin entry for a country this size is a statement about who has looked, not about what happened. When a large country has no national inquiry, ask who would have to agree to call one, and which organisations' files it would be allowed to open.

ETH.mechanism: Adoptions multiplied because of demand abroad rather than need at home, and the route closed one buyer at a time.
ETH.story:
In 2002, 262 Ethiopian children were adopted abroad. By 2008 the figure was more than 3,887 a year, American visas for Ethiopian adoptees peaked at 2,514 in 2010, and 33,303 children went abroad between 2003 and 2022. Nothing happened to Ethiopian families in those six years to multiply the number of children without parents by fifteen. What grew was demand in wealthy countries and the number of agencies and orphanages earning money per placement, and the paperwork was made to fit: Canadian families reported that their children's papers described them as orphans when their parents were alive. The US State Department found one agency, Better Futures Adoption Services, involved in child trafficking, and it lost its Ethiopian licence in February 2011.

The buyers then withdrew one at a time. Ireland's adoption authority suspended Ethiopian adoptions in October 2007, a Dutch agency stopped in September 2009, Australia suspended in December 2009 and Denmark in March 2016 after inspections. Each of those decisions removed one market while leaving the system in place for the others. Ethiopia suspended foreign adoptions itself in November 2017 and its parliament banned adoption by foreigners in January 2018, effective that February, citing the abuse and neglect of children after they left — the trigger was an American couple's 2013 conviction over the death of an adopted Ethiopian girl. The country that was supplying children was the last party to shut the door.

War then put children in reach of soldiers. During the Tigray war that began in 2020, a commission of human rights experts appointed by the UN documented in October 2022 widespread sexual violence by Ethiopian and Eritrean forces in Tigray, and rapes by Tigrayan forces of women and girls as young as 11 in Amhara villages such as Chenna in 2021. The BBC reported in February 2021 that 200 girls under 18 had registered at health facilities in Mekelle as rape survivors, which is a count of those who reached a clinic in a war zone and so is a floor rather than a total. UN monitors verified sexual violence against 73 children in Ethiopia in 2024, 38 of those attributed to the national army.

Children are also moved out for work: the 2025 US trafficking report says organised begging rings exploit Ethiopian women and children in Saudi Arabia, and Ethiopian girls are held in domestic servitude and sex trafficking in Djibouti and Sudan, sometimes controlled with drugs, with reports of official involvement continuing.

Ethiopia shows what it looks like when supply is organised around someone else's demand. When a country's adoptions rise from hundreds to thousands within a few years, ask what changed in the receiving countries rather than in the children, and who collected a fee for each placement.

MMR.mechanism: Where the people with power over children are the army or the clergy, the only bodies that could investigate them are the ones protecting them, so the findings come from outside the country altogether.
MMR.story:
In 2012, at Buthidaung prison in Myanmar's Rakhine State, Rohingya men and boys, some as young as twelve, were held and subjected to sexual violence. During the army's 2017 clearance operations in the same state, hundreds of Rohingya women and girls were raped, and in 80 per cent of the cases investigators could corroborate it was a gang rape. A fact-finding mission set up by the UN reported in August 2019 that sexual violence was a hallmark of the army's operations in Rakhine, Kachin and Shan. Note where that finding came from: the army is the state's own armed force, so the police, prosecutors and courts that would normally investigate all answer to the institution accused, and a UN mission with no power of arrest was the only body able to establish the facts. UN monitors verified the abduction of 85 children in 2024, 41 by the armed forces and allied militias and 33 by the Kachin Independence Army, mostly to make them fight.

The war also emptied villages, and people with nothing are easy to recruit. Human Rights Watch reported in March 2019 that women and girls from Kachin and northern Shan States, many of them living in displacement camps, were being sold for US$3,000 to $13,000 to families in China, then locked up and raped until they became pregnant. The price tells you the purpose: the buyer wants a baby, and the woman is the means. The traffickers were often relatives or acquaintances — one survivor was trafficked at 16 by her sister-in-law — because the trade depends on someone the family already trusts. Human Rights Watch said authorities on both sides of the border were looking away, which left traffickers little reason to fear arrest.

Children were also reached inside institutions meant to educate them. As many as 300,000 children may live in Myanmar's monasteries, TIME reported, with few records kept of who they are. At the Saitta Thuka monastery in Pathein, four girls aged 10 to 14 were staying free of charge so that they could attend school; from June 2017 they were repeatedly raped by the monk who administered the monastery, according to the children and families interviewed by Myanmar Now. When their parents went to the police in February 2018 he disappeared. Police issued orders to arrest him on sight across several regions, but TIME found officers deferring to the religious affairs ministry and the monks' governing council on whether a monk could be pursued at all.

Free board is the reason those four girls were in that building, and poverty is the reason the Kachin trade had willing recruiters. When a report says police deferred to someone, find out who that was and what they decided, because that is where the case actually ended.

SSD.mechanism: Almost everyone accused here answers to someone outside the country — a troop-contributing government, an aid agency, a national army — and South Sudan's own courts are not the ones deciding.
SSD.story:
In Malakal, displaced people live in what the UN calls a Protection of Civilians site: a camp inside a UN base, where food, medical care and shelter are handed out by international staff. In September 2022 The New Humanitarian and Al Jazeera reported that between 2015 and 2022 aid workers at that site had exploited displaced women and girls, including by trading aid for sex, and that women and girls said they had been raped and had become pregnant. Staff of the International Organization for Migration, Médecins Sans Frontières, the World Food Programme and World Vision were among those named; these are findings by journalists, not by a court. Whoever decides who goes on a distribution list can set a price that has nothing to do with money.

The national army appears more often in the UN's own counts than anyone else. Monitors verified sexual violence against 94 girls in South Sudan in 2022, some as young as seven. Seventy-four of those were attributed to the South Sudan People's Defence Forces, the state's army, with ten and four more to two factions of the armed opposition and two to the National Police Service. In 2024 they verified seven cases, five of them by the army again.

When the accused is a peacekeeper, South Sudan's courts have no part in it. Soldiers serving in UN missions can be prosecuted only by the country that sent them; the UN itself can investigate and send a soldier home, and that is the end of its power. The Secretary-General's 2025 report on the subject shows how little usually follows: one Togolese officer was repatriated and given 60 days' imprisonment, while other cases sit marked as pending additional information from the member state, meaning the sending government has not answered.

Very little of this reaches the systems that produce world figures. In 2025 the American tip line that receives reports of online child abuse logged 863 reports for South Sudan out of 23.4 million worldwide. That number mostly measures how many people in a country use the big American platforms that send reports to the tip line, so a country with little connectivity and few investigators will look almost empty however much is happening in it.

South Sudan's record was written by UN monitors and reporters because the institutions that would normally write it are among the accused. When a case involves foreign troops or foreign staff, the question is not what the local court will do but which government holds the file — and whether that government has ever finished one.

PAN.mechanism: When a state pays other people to house children and does not inspect them, the abuse is only ever found by someone who decides to go and look.
PAN.story:
Panama's state children's agency, Senniaf, places children judged to be at social risk in shelters called albergues. The shelters are run by private groups and non-governmental organisations; the state pays for the places and is meant to supervise them. In early February 2021 a subcommission of Panama's National Assembly reported that children in those shelters had been abused. By March the public prosecutor's office had opened 18 criminal investigations, inspected 57 shelters, interviewed about 280 children and identified 20 victims, who were moved; five people had been charged with offences including child mistreatment, embezzlement and sexual offences. Embezzlement sitting in that list is not a coincidence, because money taken from a shelter shows up as food not bought and staff not hired. The Ombudsman found irregularities in 34 per cent of 52 shelters inspected, found that 70 per cent of 44 shelters lacked suitable staff, and said Senniaf did little follow-up. Notice how all of those numbers came to exist: legislators and the Ombudsman physically went to the buildings. Nothing in the arrangement produced them by itself.

Panama is also a stop on routes other people run. In Cartagena, Colombia, Liliana del Carmen Campos Puello, known as La Madame, ran a network from an apartment in Bocagrande that supplied young women and minors to parties on yachts, in hotels and at beaches, and sent women on to Panama, Mexico, Miami and the Bahamas, coached on how to get past attention at airports. Sending them one at a time is the point, because border officers look for groups. In 2018 she accepted charges of human trafficking and conspiracy in a plea deal and was sentenced to eight years and one month. At hearings she threatened to name politicians and powerful men she said were clients, which is her claim and has not been verified.

The newer route is a game. In October 2024 Panama's police and public prosecutors arrested a man in Puerto Caimito, in the district of La Chorrera, accused of making illicit contact with children through the Roblox gaming platform and then threatening them to demand abuse images of themselves. The tip came from Spanish police working on a separate network, which is how most of these cases start: not from the children, and not from the platform. Separately, 5,275 web addresses of abuse material actioned by the Internet Watch Foundation in 2025 were hosted on servers in Panama.

When a government contracts out the care of children, inspection is the only thing standing between a contract and a closed building nobody visits. Ask how often an inspector calls at a shelter in Panama now, and who reads the report when one does.

TCD.mechanism: Calling a child an orphan from a war in the next country is what makes the child movable, because nobody expects anyone to produce the parents.
TCD.story:
In October 2007, at Abéché in eastern Chad, members of a French charity called Zoé's Ark were stopped as they prepared to put 103 children on a plane to host families in France. The charity said the children were orphans from Darfur, the war in neighbouring Sudan. That description is the device the whole operation rested on. An orphan from a war across a border has no family anyone is expected to find, no reliable papers and a nationality that is hard to check, so a child who is none of those things becomes transportable the moment someone writes it down. Chadian authorities checked, and found that most of the children were Chadian and not orphans.

On 26 December 2007 a Chadian court convicted six French members of attempting to kidnap the children, sentenced them to eight years' forced labour and ordered each of them to pay €60,000 to each of the 103 children. A Chadian and a Sudanese defendant received four years and two Chadians were acquitted. The six French members were then transferred to France to serve their sentences, and at the end of March 2008 Chad's president, Idriss Déby, pardoned them. The convictions stand on paper; no one served the sentence, and the compensation went with it.

Chad's own army appears in the UN's records. Monitors verified rape and other sexual violence against three girls by the Chadian National Army in Lac Province in 2022, and in Sudan attributed four of 35 cases of sexual violence against girls aged 12 to 17 to the same army. In the Lake Chad basin they verified the abduction of 191 children in Lac Province and Diffa. These counts come from UN verification teams, which confirm what they can reach and record nothing about the rest.

Outside those cases, almost nothing about Chad has been measured. Childlight's 2026 update, which gathers survey data on the online sexual exploitation of children, found that West and Central Africa, where Chad sits, has no representative surveys at all — meaning no one has asked a sample of children there directly, so there is no rate to compare with anywhere else.

When an organisation says it is moving children who are orphans from a war zone, the question is who verified it and whether anyone went looking for the families. And when a conviction is followed by a transfer and a pardon, the sentence is not the end of the story; what the defendants actually served is.

GIN.mechanism: In a camp, aid is the only income, so the person holding the ration list holds an employer's power — and when the agency investigates itself, 'unsubstantiated' describes the evidence an investigator could gather, not what happened.
GIN.story:
In 2001 and 2002 a joint team from UNHCR, the UN's refugee agency, and Save the Children UK visited refugee camps in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone. Its report in early 2002 said refugee children were being sexually exploited by employees of non-governmental organisations, of UNHCR and of other UN bodies, by peacekeepers and by community leaders, often in exchange for food and aid. The reason aid works as payment is that inside a camp there is nothing else: no jobs, no market, no money of one's own. A staff member deciding who is on a distribution list is in the position of an employer who also controls the housing.

The UN then investigated itself. Its Office of Internal Oversight Services fully investigated 43 cases and substantiated 10, among them the rape of a 14-year-old refugee girl in a camp in Guinea and a sexual relationship between a UN Volunteer and a girl of about 15 in Guéckédou. One substantiated case involved a peacekeeper, who was repatriated, which means sent home to his own country and is the furthest the UN's own powers reach. In October 2002 the investigators reported that no allegation against a UN staff member had been substantiated and that they had found no evidence of widespread abuse. Save the Children UK answered that nothing the UN had found made it think it had been wrong.

The gap between 43 cases examined and 10 substantiated is worth sitting with. To substantiate an allegation an investigator has to assemble enough evidence to be sure of it. The witnesses here were displaced children without documents, often interviewed through interpreters employed by the same organisations, in camps the investigators visited briefly and the staff lived in. An unsubstantiated finding records what that process could stand up; it is not a finding that the child was wrong.

Little has been measured in Guinea since. Childlight's 2026 update found that West and Central Africa has no representative surveys of children on technology-facilitated sexual exploitation, so there is no figure for how common any of this is now.

Guinea is the case to remember when an institution announces the results of looking into itself. Ask who chose the investigators, who they could interview and in front of whom, and whether anyone outside the organisation was allowed to look as well.

MWI.mechanism: A poor country becomes the place other systems empty into: a church can post an accused man there, and a camp built for a fifth of the people in it keeps no record of who is inside.
MWI.story:
A missionary posting is a job a church can create anywhere in the world, and the church decides who fills it. In 2006 police in Slovenia detained a Catholic priest, Father Franc Frantar, over the abuse of up to 16 minors. He did not stay to be prosecuted; he went to Malawi as a missionary, and he came back only after Interpol, the organisation through which national police forces circulate wanted notices, issued one for him. From Malawi's side nothing visible happened at all. A priest arrived to work, and nobody in the country had been told what he was accused of at home, which is what makes the move effective: it is not a disappearance, it is a transfer into a place with no reason to be suspicious.

The larger record in Malawi is a camp. Dzaleka was built for 10,000 people and holds about 53,000. At that density nobody knows reliably who lives where, and the informal bars and housing that spring up are not places any authority has a list for. The 2025 US trafficking report says organised transnational criminal groups working out of those bars and compounds recruit girls for sex trafficking inside the camp and in roadside bars along the highway to the capital, Lilongwe. The camp is also a waypoint on what is called the Southern Route, used to move people towards South Africa. That matters for a child: in a place where everyone is understood to be passing through, a girl who is gone is assumed to have travelled on. Girls are also exploited in bars and illegal brothels in Lilongwe and Blantyre, and the report says officials' own involvement continued to obstruct enforcement.

Malawi shows the receiving end of two different systems, one religious and one criminal, and in both cases the thing that made it work was the absence of a record. Ask who was told when a foreign priest took up a posting, and who holds the list of children inside Dzaleka.

SVN.mechanism: Leaving the country defeats a prosecution without anyone having to defeat the evidence, because a court cannot try a defendant it cannot compel to appear.
SVN.story:
Slovenian police detained Father Franc Frantar, a Catholic priest, in 2006 over the abuse of up to 16 minors. He was not acquitted and the case was not dropped. He left for Malawi, in southern Africa, to work as a missionary, and that was enough to stop the prosecution for years. A criminal trial needs the defendant in the room, and a prosecutor who wants him back has to ask the country he is in to extradite him, which takes a treaty, a formal request and a foreign court's agreement. Meanwhile the evidence ages: the witnesses were children, their memories are tested on the stand years later, and each year of delay is worth something to the defence. Frantar returned only after Interpol issued a notice for him to police forces worldwide. Nothing about the departure required secrecy or force. It required a church willing to offer a posting abroad to a priest under investigation, and nobody with the authority to say no.

Slovenia also appears in a much older record, on the receiving side of a state programme. Between 1940 and 1945 Nazi Germany seized children in occupied Poland and elsewhere whom it judged racially valuable, held them in homes run by an SS organisation called Lebensborn, and placed them with German families under new identities. This was office work as much as abduction: files, assessments and fresh paperwork, which is what made the placements hard to reverse after the war, since a child with new papers has no documented parents. In 1947 and 1948 an American military tribunal at Nuremberg tried fourteen officials of the SS race and settlement office, Lebensborn and related bodies, partly for the kidnapping of those children; it convicted thirteen and acquitted one.

Both of Slovenia's entries turn on movement rather than concealment. When you read that a priest under investigation was posted abroad, ask who in the church arranged it, whether anyone in the receiving country was warned, and what the prosecutor at home did on the day he found out.

XKX.mechanism: A large foreign presence with money and legal immunity is not a side market for a trafficking business; it is the market the business was built to serve.
XKX.story:
NATO troops and UN administrators arrived in Kosovo in 1999. Within a few years Kosovo had become a major destination for women and girls trafficked for forced prostitution, and Amnesty International's report of May 2004 put a figure on why: the international presence generated 80 per cent of traffickers' income at that time. Soldiers of the NATO force, UN police and international civilian staff were men on foreign salaries in a place where very little money was circulating otherwise. A business needs customers who can pay, and for a few years in Kosovo those were the customers.

The supply came from outside. Women and girls were brought mainly from Moldova, Romania, Ukraine and Russia through Serbia, and local girls were abducted as well. The UN's own peacekeeping department acknowledged in 2004 that peacekeepers had, as it put it, come to be seen as part of the problem in trafficking rather than the solution.

Almost nothing followed for the buyers, and the reason is a rule rather than a failure of will in any one case. Soldiers serving in a foreign mission are normally subject only to the courts of the country that sent them: the host country cannot prosecute them, and the mission can at most send a man home. So the decision to charge a soldier who bought sex from a trafficked girl in Kosovo lay with his own government, thousands of kilometres away, with no witnesses, no complainant and nothing to gain politically from pursuing it. Amnesty found no evidence of criminal proceedings against any military personnel in their home countries.

Kosovo is the case that shows demand being created by the people sent to restore order, and then protected by the terms on which they came. When an international mission arrives anywhere, ask which country would have to try its soldiers for a crime against a local child, and whether that country has ever done it.

COG.mechanism: A soldier sent abroad on a UN mission can be prosecuted only by the country that sent him, so the only file that matters is the one in his own capital.
COG.story:
From September to December 2015 a contingent of soldiers from the Republic of Congo guarded the airport at Bambari, in the Central African Republic, as part of the UN peacekeeping mission there known as MINUSCA. In January 2016 researchers from Human Rights Watch working in Bambari documented eight cases of sexual exploitation and abuse by MINUSCA peacekeepers, among them a 14-year-old girl and an 18-year-old woman who said they had been gang-raped near the airport. Most of the incidents happened during the months that contingent held the airport. Survivors believed the soldiers were from the Republic of Congo or from DR Congo, and Human Rights Watch linked the airport cases to the Republic of Congo's contingent. These are the findings of a rights organisation, not of any court.

What happens next is set by the terms on which troops are lent to the UN. The UN can investigate, and it can repatriate a soldier, meaning put him on a plane home. It cannot prosecute him. Criminal jurisdiction stays with the contributing country, so the only authority that could charge these soldiers sits in Brazzaville — not in the Central African Republic, where the children were, and not at the UN. For the victims that means the case leaves the country with the accused, and whether anything happens depends on a government answering questions about its own army, at home, where no one is watching.

Inside Congo-Brazzaville itself there is almost nothing to measure against. Childlight's 2026 update, which collects survey data on the online sexual exploitation of children, found that West and Central Africa has no representative surveys, so there is no national rate for anything of this kind.

A country can appear on this map purely as the home address of accused soldiers, and that is the position Congo-Brazzaville is in. When troops are sent abroad to protect civilians, the power to punish them travels home with them. Ask whether their government ever reported back on these cases, and what happened to the men who guarded Bambari airport.

ISL.mechanism: Hosting is a service strangers buy by the month, so a hosting ranking records where files are stored rather than where children were harmed.
ISL.story:
Iceland is on this map mostly as an address for machines. A server is a computer in a building, rented by the month; the person renting it can be anywhere, and the children in the files can be anywhere else again. In 2025 the Internet Watch Foundation, a British organisation that finds and removes child sexual abuse material from the internet, actioned 7,455 web addresses hosted in Iceland, about 2 per cent of everything it dealt with that year.

Two police operations in 2025 show what sits on such machines and how it is sold. The first concerned Kidflix, a paid platform created in 2021 that let users stream abuse videos as well as download them, paying in cryptocurrency that was converted into site tokens. Streaming is the change worth noticing: a customer who only watches never has the files on his own computer, which is what most police searches look for. Users uploaded 91,000 unique videos, 6,288 hours in all, and the platform had 1.8 million users between 2022 and 2025. German and Dutch authorities seized the server on 11 March 2025, when it still held about 72,000 videos. The wider operation, led by Bavarian police with Europol and 38 countries, identified 1,393 suspects and arrested 79; the record for this case counts 39 children. Europol called it the largest child sexual exploitation operation in its history.

The second was a Danish-led case. A Danish man arrested in November 2024 ran a paid platform distributing abuse material generated by artificial intelligence, which he produced himself; users paid a small fee for a password. Most of the arrests came on 26 February 2025 in an operation involving 18 other countries, with 273 suspects identified and 25 arrested. Europol noted that many countries have no law covering material a computer generated rather than recorded, which is why that platform could operate openly enough to charge for passwords. Everyone arrested in both operations is charged, not convicted.

A country's place on a hosting list says something about its internet industry, not its population. When you see one, ask which companies rent out that space, how quickly they act when told what is on it, and whether any law requires them to look.

JAM.mechanism: Jamaica is measured by a survey of children rather than by a count of cases, and the adults who would normally report are often the ones being paid.
JAM.story:
Almost everything on this map is a case: it exists because someone reported, an investigator opened a file and a court or an inquiry wrote something down. Jamaica has a different kind of figure. A prevalence study in 2023 estimated that 6.3 per cent of Jamaican children aged 12 to 17 had experienced conditions indicating they had been trafficked. A prevalence study asks a representative sample of children directly, which means it reaches children who never told anyone, were never believed or had nowhere to go. That is why a survey figure is always far larger than a courts figure, and why the two should never be compared as if they measured the same thing.

The 2025 US trafficking report, which cites that study, describes where it happens: children are sexually exploited in resort areas visited by tourists, sometimes with a parent taking part, and in some communities men pay girls, or pay their families, for sex. The people named as arranging it are family members, local power brokers known as dons, and buyers both foreign and Jamaican. Family involvement changes the whole shape of the problem. Every protection designed for children assumes an adult who will notice and report; where the adult is receiving the payment, that assumption produces nothing, and a teacher or nurse who suspects something has no parent to call.

The report also says that corruption and the involvement of officials, including inside law enforcement, remained significant concerns. That removes the other route. Reporting is only safe if the person receiving the report has no stake in the trade, and in a small resort town a parent cannot know which officer at the station that is.

Jamaica is one of the few countries here with a measured estimate of how many of its children this reaches, which is more than most governments have produced. Use it as the question to ask elsewhere: has anyone surveyed the children, and what has ever happened to an officer accused of protecting a buyer?

MNG.mechanism: Mongolia's whole entry rests on one foreign government's annual summary, which describes what is happening without counting any of it.
MNG.story:
What is known here comes from a single kind of document, so it is worth knowing what that document is. Each year the US State Department publishes a report assessing other governments' efforts against human trafficking, written from embassy reporting, local organisations and officials. It is a description, not a tally: it names practices and places, and it almost never gives case numbers, court outcomes or a rate. For Mongolia that report is the record.

It says that women and girls are sex-trafficked in Mongolian hotels, massage parlours, illegal brothels, bars and karaoke clubs, mostly in Ulaanbaatar, the capital, and in provincial centres and towns on the borders, and that this is sometimes made easier by police not enforcing the law. It says some families are complicit, which means the adult who would ordinarily intervene is part of the arrangement.

It also describes how the approach happens now. Traffickers use online platforms to groom children — building a friendly relationship first, then asking for a sexual image — and then blackmail them with what the child has already sent. The image is the mechanism: once it exists, the trafficker no longer needs to persuade anyone, because the child's fear of the picture being shown does the work, and that fear is also why the child does not tell a parent or a teacher.

A third practice is a permit used for something other than its purpose. Children taken abroad for competitions have instead been put to work, for example as horse jockeys. Everything about that journey looks legitimate at a border: a child, an accompanying adult, an event.

When a country's entry is built from an outside government's yearly summary, you are reading a description of a problem that nobody local has counted. Ask whether Mongolian police have opened cases against the hotels and clubs the report describes, and what happens to an officer who does not enforce the law.

LUX.mechanism: Adoption was supplied to a quota set by demand in the receiving countries, and each receiving country's share of that demand was small enough to look harmless from inside it.
LUX.story:
Between 1984 and 2008, 561 South Korean children were adopted into families in Luxembourg. They were part of about 163,898 children South Korea sent abroad between 1953 and 2008. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found that the state had enabled fraud in those overseas adoptions, and described how the system worked. Agencies sent children abroad in set numbers to meet demand from foreign agencies, and some children who had known, living parents were registered as orphans.

The set number is the part that explains the rest. A quota has to be filled whether or not that many children need new families, so somebody has to find the shortfall, and the paperwork has to be made to match. Pressure of that kind does not come from the sending country alone. It is the sum of the orders placed by every receiving country, and Luxembourg's 561 children were part of that sum.

That is Luxembourg's part in this, and it is not a passive one. Each of those adoptions had to be approved at the Luxembourg end as well as in Seoul, by people reading documents that said a child had no family able to raise them. Nobody in Luxembourg was in a position to verify that claim, and nobody had to.

A small receiving country's record looks like a rounding error until you see what it was ordering. If you know someone adopted from Korea in those years, their file may not describe where they came from. Ask whether Luxembourg has ever examined its own adoption records, as the Netherlands did in 2021, and what an adoptee can get out of them today.

CRI.mechanism: Flight ends a prosecution without touching the evidence, because a trial needs the defendant in the room and getting him back needs another country's agreement.
CRI.story:
In 2018, as accusations of child abuse against him became public, Father Mauricio Víquez, a Costa Rican Catholic priest, left the country. He travelled through Panama and on to Mexico. For a prosecutor that is often the end of it, and not because the case has weakened. A criminal trial requires the defendant to be present, so once he is abroad the file simply stops moving, and the only way to restart it is to ask the country he is in to hand him over.

That request is called extradition, and it needs several things to line up at once. There has to be an agreement between the two countries allowing it; the conduct has to be a crime in both; the requesting country has to put together enough evidence to satisfy a foreign judge; and the courts in the country holding him have to agree, which can take years of hearings the fugitive is entitled to contest. Any one of those failing leaves him where he is. This is why leaving works so reliably, and why a church or an employer that moves someone abroad has done something more consequential than merely relocating him.

In this case it did not work. Víquez was caught in Mexico and extradited in 2021, and in 2022 a Costa Rican court sentenced him to 20 years. Two governments cooperated, the conditions held, and the trial that had been suspended for three years took place.

Costa Rica's single entry here is the version of this story where the machinery worked. When someone accused of abusing children leaves a country, ask how they were able to go, whether anyone with a duty to report had told the police first, and whether the country they went to has ever sent anyone back.

CPV.mechanism: Measuring how often children are exploited online means asking children, and nobody has asked them here — so Cape Verde has no rate at all, rather than a low one.
CPV.story:
To know how often children in a country are sexually exploited online, somebody has to ask the children. Police figures cannot answer it, because they only contain the cases that were reported, and most are not. What answers it is a representative survey: a sample of children chosen so that their answers can be scaled up to the whole population, asked carefully enough that they will tell the truth to a stranger.

That is a demanding thing to run. It needs money, trained interviewers, rules for what to do when a child discloses abuse during the interview, and a government willing to let the questions be asked at all. Childlight's 2026 update, which gathers this evidence worldwide, rests on representative surveys from only 60 countries. West and Central Africa, where Cape Verde sits, has none of them, and neither does South Asia or the Middle East and North Africa.

So the honest description of Cape Verde's entry is not that little happens here. It is that no measurement exists. Nobody has asked a sample of Cape Verdean children anything, which means there is no rate to compare with the rates from the 60 countries that have been surveyed, and no way to tell whether a figure borrowed from elsewhere would be close or badly wrong.

This matters beyond one country, because world totals still get published. When a global figure covers places with no survey, those places are either left out of it, which makes the total too low, or filled in with a rate measured somewhere else, which makes the total a projection presented as a count. Where this map shades a country by estimate, that is what has happened.

An empty entry is a fact about the people doing the counting, not about the children. Ask who would pay for a survey of children in Cape Verde and who would be allowed to run it, and ask which agency a Cape Verdean child's report would reach if they made one tomorrow.

DZA.mechanism: The two global systems that could place Algeria somewhere both depend on someone volunteering information — a government sending its figures, or researchers surveying children — and neither has happened.
DZA.story:
The United Nations does not count trafficking. Its 2024 global report covered 156 countries, but only 72 of them supplied data for 2023, because the report is assembled from figures that national governments choose to send in: their own police investigations, prosecutions and identified victims. A government that does not answer is not in that year's numbers, and nothing in the system distinguishes between a country with nothing to report, a country where no agency compiles such figures, and a country that compiles them and keeps them.

The other way to place a country is to ask its children directly, through a representative survey — a sample large and carefully chosen enough that the answers describe the whole population. Childlight's 2026 update, which collects that evidence, found that the Middle East and North Africa, the region Algeria belongs to, has no such surveys. South Asia and West and Central Africa have none either.

Algeria therefore sits outside both systems at once. There is no survey of Algerian children to give a rate, and no national return in the UN's dataset to give a count of cases, so the country cannot be ranked, compared or tracked over time. That is not the same as evidence of safety. It is the absence of any instrument pointed at the question.

The third major source, an American tip line for online abuse material, has its own hole of exactly this kind: of the 23.4 million reports it received in 2025, 14 per cent could not be assigned to any country at all, because nobody could work out where the person or the device was.

Blank countries are produced by how the counting is organised, and the organisation of it is visible and fixable. Ask whether Algeria submits trafficking figures to the UN and who inside the government would prepare them, and ask what institution an Algerian child who was exploited online would actually be able to tell.

MDV.mechanism: The largest number in the online part of this map is a count of reports from American technology companies, so it measures which apps a country's children use as much as what is happening to them.
MDV.story:
In 2025 the American tip line that receives reports of online child sexual abuse logged 23.4 million of them. That figure drives much of what is known about abuse online, so it matters how it is produced. Most of those reports come from technology companies, mainly American ones, which are required under US law to report abuse material they find on their own services. Each report is a company telling the tip line what it found.

Two things follow. A country's report count rises with how many of its people use those particular platforms, so a country whose children mostly use other apps, or have less internet access, will appear almost empty. And it rises with how hard each company chooses to look, since a company that does not search its own service has nothing to report. Where the country cannot be worked out at all, the report is unplaceable, as 14 per cent of the 2025 reports were.

For the Maldives there is nothing to check such a count against. Childlight's 2026 update, which assembles representative surveys of children about online sexual exploitation, found that South Asia, the region the Maldives belongs to, has no such surveys at all. A representative survey is the only instrument that reaches children who never reported anything to anyone, and without one there is no national rate to set beside the number of reports an American tip line happened to receive.

So the Maldives appears on this map as a country where none of the available instruments has been used: no survey of children, and only whatever volume of reports the platform companies produced.

A report count is a measure of detection, not of abuse. Ask which platforms children in the Maldives actually use and whether those companies report anything to anyone, and ask who inside the country receives a report when a child does make one.

OMN.mechanism: When a country is shaded by estimate, a rate measured in other countries has been applied to this one, and the low numbers that do exist measure reporting rather than safety.
OMN.story:
An estimate is not a weaker count. It is a different thing: a rate measured somewhere else, applied to a population here. Where this map shades a country by estimate rather than by documented cases, that is the operation being performed, and it is worth knowing how far the borrowed rate has travelled. Childlight's 2026 update on the online sexual exploitation of children rests on representative surveys from only 60 countries. The Middle East and North Africa, the region Oman belongs to, has none. So any figure for Oman has been carried in from countries with different internet access, different household structures and different willingness to answer a stranger's questions about sex, and nothing in the method tells you whether the transfer is sound.

The alternative source would be a government's own figures. The UN's 2024 global report on trafficking covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied data for 2023, because governments send those figures voluntarily. Absence from that list says nothing about what happened and everything about what was filed.

The reason this cannot be waved away as pedantry is that small numbers get read as good news. In 2025 North Korea generated twelve reports to the American tip line that collects reports of online abuse material from technology companies. Nobody would present that as evidence that North Korean children are safe; it reflects a country almost entirely outside the services that generate reports. The same logic applies wherever a count is low, and it has to be applied before the number means anything.

An estimate is a placeholder for a measurement nobody has made. Ask whether Oman has ever asked a sample of its own children directly, who would run such a survey, and whether the government sends trafficking figures to the UN at all.

STP.mechanism: A number only exists if a chain of people exists to produce it — a child who tells someone, an official who records it, an agency that keeps the file — and where the chain is missing, so is the country.
STP.story:
Every figure in this field starts as a chain of people. A child tells someone. That person tells an official. The official records it in a form that someone later adds up. Alternatively a researcher asks a sample of children directly and publishes a rate. Where neither chain exists, nothing enters any count anywhere, and the country appears as a blank that looks like calm.

For São Tomé and Príncipe, the research chain has not been built. Childlight's 2026 update, which gathers representative surveys of children on technology-facilitated sexual exploitation, found that West and Central Africa has none, so there is no rate for the region to place São Tomé and Príncipe within. The official chain is thin in the same way worldwide: the UN's 2024 global trafficking report covered 156 countries, but only 72 sent in data for 2023, because the figures are supplied voluntarily by governments. And of the 23.4 million reports the main American tip line received in 2025, 14 per cent could not be attributed to any country at all.

This is not only a problem of small or poor countries. Italy, Brazil, the Philippines and India have some of the largest Catholic populations in the world and, in the sources reached here, none of them has held a national inquiry into abuse in institutions. Those countries have courts, budgets and statisticians. What they lack is a body that was given the job and the power to demand the files, which is the same thing São Tomé and Príncipe lacks, at a different scale.

A blank country is a description of the machinery, not of childhood there. Ask who in São Tomé and Príncipe would run a survey of children and who would fund it, whether the police have anyone whose job is to record these offences, and where a child's report would end up if one were made this week.
